stances.claim: Arbitration is becoming a popular mode of settling local and international disputes -- the SC encourages it because it speedily dispenses justice and helps unclog judicial dockets; parties select their own judges, one case per tribunal, with decisions final and unappealable

PH has participated in several arbitration cases and won notable ones -- Naia III vs Piatco at ICC Paris, Naia III vs Fraport AG at ICSID Washington -- and is pursuing its most important case at Itlos Hamburg against China on the Spratlys/West Philippine Sea, with decision expected early next year

The MWSS won its arbitration vs Manila Water but lost vs Maynilad (ICC Paris appointed both panel chairs); it promptly obeyed and enforced its win but refused to obey its loss, arguing it had a duty to set 'just and equitable rates' -- palpably unreasonable since it freely participated with full knowledge of the finality and binding effect of whatever decisions may be rendered

Just because the government exercises indisputable sovereignty and commands the police and military, it should not impose its will arbitrarily -- it must set the example in following arbitral decisions regardless of outcome and lead in observing the rule of law

How can PH expect China to accept an unfavorable Itlos decision if PH itself refuses to accept arbitral decisions unfavorable to it? PH would be a worse violator of the rule of law because it willingly and actively participated while China did not -- 'what is good for the goose should also be good for the gander'

The Camp John Hay arbitration between BCDA and CJHDevCo (via Philippine Dispute Resolution Center Inc.) ended in a draw -- both parties mutually breached; the lease was rescinded; CJHDevCo delivers the leased area to BCDA; BCDA returns to CJHDevCo all rentals (~P1.5 billion); but the arbitral decision did not touch on rights of the innocent bystanders

Investors, locators, and condominium owners -- who paid CJHDevCo in good faith for rights over homes, condominiums, golf-club shares -- are innocent bystanders whose payments cannot dissipate into nothingness; BCDA should treat them reasonably, equitably, and fairly because the lease became invalid only after February 2015 rescission

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the arbitration-decisions doctrinal anchor for the West Philippine Sea case and beyond. Arbitration is becoming a popular mode of settling local and international disputes -- the Supreme Court encourages it because it speedily dispenses justice and helps unclog judicial dockets. Unlike in judicial cases, the arbitral parties select their judges: usually each side nominates one judge, and the arbitral body that conducts the arbitration chooses the third judge who becomes the panel chair. Every arbitral tribunal handles only one case at a time; its decision is final and unappealable. PH has participated in several arbitration cases. It won its arbitration concerning the construction and operation of Naia III against Piatco; the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in Paris selected the panel chair. It won another Naia III arbitration against Fraport AG, a German company; the International Center for the Settlement of Disputes (ICSID) in Washington appointed the panel chair. PH's most important arbitration involves the Spratlys and other isles in the West Philippine Sea: PH sued China at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos) in Hamburg. China is a member of the international group that created Itlos and has a judge sitting on the tribunal -- but it refused to participate, claiming 'indisputable sovereignty.' Itlos continued the proceedings and is poised to issue its decision early next year; PH is confident it will win. The problem: will China, given its superior military clout, respect and obey an Itlos decision dislodging it from those isles? RULE OF LAW: the government, through MWSS, likewise won its arbitration against Manila Water but lost to Maynilad in a separate case; the ICC, like in Naia III, appointed the chair of both panels. MWSS promptly obeyed and enforced its win over Manila Water but refused to obey its loss to Maynilad, arguing it had a duty to set 'just and equitable rates.' In stark contrast, Manila Water laudably accepted its loss while reserving compensation rights under its concession agreement with MWSS. MWSS's double-faced stance is palpably unreasonable: it freely participated in both cases with full knowledge of the finality and binding effect of whatever decisions may be rendered -- it cannot accept and obey only the decision it won. That is the worst kind of selective justice. Just because it exercises indisputable sovereignty and commands the police and military, the government should not impose its will arbitrarily -- it must set the example in following arbitral decisions regardless of outcome and lead in observing the rule of law. Otherwise, how can our government expect China to accept and obey an Itlos decision unfavorable to China if our government refuses to accept arbitral decisions unfavorable to it? PH would be a worse violator of the rule of law than China because it willingly and actively participated while China did not. What is good for the goose should also be good for the gander. INNOCENT BYSTANDERS: the arbitration between BCDA and CJH Development Corp. (CJHDevCo) -- with the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center Inc. as arbitral body -- ended in a draw. The tribunal held that both parties mutually breached their lease agreement over Camp John Hay in Baguio; it rescinded the agreement and directed CJHDevCo to deliver the leased area (with all improvements and constructions) to BCDA, which in turn was ordered to return to CJHDevCo all the rentals paid, almost P1.5 billion. While the arbitral decision settled the BCDA-CJHDevCo dispute, it did not touch on the rights and obligations of the investors, locators, and condominium owners in Camp John Hay who were not parties to the arbitration but had in good faith paid CJHDevCo for their rights over homes, condominiums, golf-club shares, and other improvements built by the developer. Their payments cannot just dissipate into nothingness -- BCDA (which was adjudged to take over) should treat them reasonably, equitably, and fairly. When they contracted with CJHDevCo, the lease was still valid and existing; it became invalid only after February 2015 rescission. As innocent bystanders not party to the arbitration, they should not be penalized and deprived of what they had paid for in good faith.
